scenes.text: One project. Many sources. Your preferred tools. Parallel agents. One approved path to production. And the client never touches the production repository.

Here is what a client hands us on a normal Tuesday. Two application repositories, a prototype built with an AI tool and exported as a zip, a brand folder with a fifty-megabyte launch video, and a note that says: can you make this work together. Most tools would make us flatten all of that into one repository. CommonForge does not. Intake runs a dry-run inventory before anything is written: it keeps the nested repositories separate, excludes dependencies, routes the large video to object storage instead of Git, and blocks a stray environment file without ever showing its contents. The result is one project the client can understand, built from resources that keep their own identity, history and permissions. The source inspector shows the real Artifacts repository behind the website and the asset manifest behind the brand folder.

Now the client. They want to improve the quote page on their own portal, and they do not want to learn Git to do it. They click Start an update. CommonForge pins the version that is actually live, not whatever is on a main branch, and publishes a working copy from an allowlist the developer configured. It is a fresh repository with a single commit. Not a branch of production. Not a fork with history. Watch the terminal. With the client's own credentials, cloning the canonical repository is denied. Cloning the edition works, and the log shows exactly one commit. A secret seeded into the real repository's old history is simply not there. The client sees a folder. The developer keeps the repository.

This is the part clients care about. They open that working copy in whatever tool they already use. Here it is Cursor. They ask for an itemised breakdown on the quote form, the tool edits the files, and that is the whole workflow. When they are done, they zip the folder and click Return changes. The platform compares the returned files against the inventory it recorded when it published the copy, so it knows precisely which two files changed. Then it enforces scope. Allowed paths are mapped back onto the real repository. Protected paths are blocked with a plain reason. If someone edits the manifest to redirect the change, that is refused as a path escape, because the manifest on the server is the authority, never the one in the folder. Two files changed, zero blocked. The client's work is now a candidate, and it has not touched production.

Meanwhile the developer's agents have been working, and this is where Artifacts earns its place. Three real agent sessions start within seconds of each other. These are live coding agents, not replays; the timestamps come from the platform's event log. Agent A has one task that spans two repositories. Its workspace holds the website and the API side by side, each a fork of the canonical repository with its own short-lived write token. It changes the quote endpoint and the interface that consumes it as one piece of work. Agent B is the client's edition from a moment ago. Agent C is replacing the logo in the asset collection and updating the written requirements. Nobody shares a writable directory. Nobody holds a token to production. When an agent submits, the platform freezes the exact commit, revokes its write token and records the candidate. One more push after that is denied. Isolation here is a credential boundary, not a convention, and that is what lets hundreds of agents share a project safely.

Now the interesting part. Integration runs in an isolated runner. Git merges all three candidates without a single textual conflict. CommonForge does not trust a clean merge. The project declares a contract between the API and the website: the shape of the quote response. Agent A changed that shape, and the website's contract test fails against the merged result. So the Change stops. Nothing is accepted, production is untouched, and the evidence panel shows exactly why: merge clean, contract failed, fourteen of fourteen tests passing elsewhere. The badge says Needs your decision. A clean merge is not proof the application works. Declared contracts and executable checks are. An agent saying the tests passed is not evidence; the runner's signed results are.

The developer sends the conflict to the repair agent. It gets a fresh isolated workspace on the current accepted version, with both candidates attached as read-only references, and reconciles the interface with the new API shape. When it resubmits, the proposal identifier changes. Every edit is a new immutable identity, so an approval given to the old version cannot ride along with the new one. Integration runs again. Contracts pass. Tests pass. Now the client gets a private preview on a separate origin, behind an expiring token, with isolated test data and outbound traffic disabled. They can actually use the quote flow, and the side-effect counters stay at zero, because nothing in a preview can reach a real database, email or payment.

Three decisions get this change to production, and they are three separate records with three separate permissions, even when one person holds all three. First the client approves the outcome. They tested the preview, it does what they asked, they click Approve. That decision is theirs. Second the developer accepts. The ledger, a Durable Object, checks in one atomic transaction that the proposal identity matches what was reviewed, that the accepted heads of all three resources are still what the candidate was built on, and that the approval is not stale. Only then do the accepted versions advance. The Git branches follow the ledger, not the other way round. Third, publishing. A separate release record binds the accepted version, the build digest and the target. The developer approves the release, the deploy runs, the health check turns green, and the live portal shows the new quote breakdown. Switch to the client's view. Same proposal identifier, same timeline, and it is live. What they do not see is a publish button. They never had that permission, and they never needed it.

One more thing, because real projects need it. Suppose the new logo was a mistake. We go to Versions, pick the previous version, and restore it. Code and assets come back together, because a version is the whole project. Restore is a new forward version, never a history rewrite. The audit trail stays intact, and it goes through the same publish gate as everything else. And nothing is locked in. Export gives you ordinary Git bundles and an asset manifest with hashes, verifiable with plain Git. No proprietary filesystem, no vendor format.
Clients work in their own tools. Agents work in isolation. Developers keep authority. One approved path to production, built on Cloudflare Workers and Artifacts. CommonForge. Build together faster.
